en.title: iPhone battery capacity: read maximum capacity as a trend before you replace the battery
en.meta: Settings shows today's maximum capacity, not how fast it is falling. How to read iPhone battery capacity, what the 80% benchmark means and when to get the battery checked. BattAI charts the values you enter with a confidence range. One purchase, not a subscription.
en.h1: iPhone battery capacity: one number is not enough, watch how it falls
en.lead: You open Settings › Battery, see a maximum capacity of 86%, and are not sure whether that is good or bad or whether it is time to replace the battery. The answer is how fast that number is dropping, not today's number on its own.
en.answer: An iPhone's battery capacity (maximum capacity) is how much charge the battery can hold now compared with when it was new, shown in Settings › Battery. Apple uses 80% as a service benchmark, but a replacement decision should look at how much it drops per month, together with cycle count and the symptoms you actually see, such as fast drain or heat.
paras: Settings only shows today's maximum capacity. A phone that has sat at 86% for half a year and one that fell from 92% to 86% in three months are very different, even though today's number is the same. Writing the number down every so often tells you more than one look.

A third-party iPhone app cannot read maximum capacity or cycle count by itself. iOS lets apps read only battery level, charge state, Low Power Mode, whole-device thermal state and time, so be wary of an app that claims to read capacity automatically. The capacity value has to come from what you enter from Settings or from the system's Analytics file.

BattAI lets you enter the maximum capacity from Settings › Battery and gives you a 0–100 battery health score right away. Each value you enter is charted with a 95% confidence range, and once readings are at least 30 days apart it calculates the monthly change. The battery card and the full, low battery and heat alerts are free; the health score, trends, reports and widgets unlock with one purchase, not a subscription. Scores are calculated, not an Apple diagnosis.
look: The app says plainly that maximum capacity is entered by you, not read from a sensor
Each value you enter is kept on a chart, not overwritten
Measured, estimated and user-entered values are kept apart
No account, and battery data stays on the device
Clear pricing with no automatic charges
steps: Open Settings › Battery and note today's maximum capacity.
Enter it in BattAI to see the score and the main factor behind it.
Enter it again every two to four weeks; once readings are 30 days apart you see the monthly drop.
Turn on the full charge alert at 80% or 90% if that suits how you use the phone.
If the number nears 80% or the battery drains unusually fast, get it checked by Apple or a service provider.
rows: Shows where you are now, not how fast it is falling
How much it drops per month
Lets you estimate when it will reach 80% before deciding on a replacement

en.fits: BattAI suits people who want to know how fast their battery capacity is falling before deciding to keep, replace the battery or sell: enter the capacity from Settings for a 0–100 score, a capacity chart with a confidence range and a resale report. The battery card and the full, low battery and heat alerts are free; the score, trends and reports unlock with one purchase. No account, no ads.
faq: At what battery capacity should I replace an iPhone battery?

Apple uses 80% as a service benchmark. If capacity is still above that but the battery drains unusually fast, or it dropped quickly within a few months, it is still worth getting checked. BattAI's score is calculated, not an Apple diagnosis.
Does BattAI read battery capacity automatically?
No. iOS does not let apps read maximum capacity. You enter the value from Settings › Battery or import it from the system's Analytics file.
Is there a monthly fee?
No. The battery card and alerts are free, and the health score, trends, reports and widgets unlock with one purchase, not a subscription.

en.title: iPhone calculator widget: calculate right on the Home Screen and find old results again
en.meta: Want to do quick sums from the Home Screen without opening an app? How to pick an iPhone calculator widget that really calculates in the widget, keeps named history and stays readable in every theme. CalDaily has one free theme and a one-time unlock, no subscription.
en.h1: Calculator widget: tap the sum on the Home Screen, then find the result again
en.lead: Splitting dinner with friends, checking a sale price at the mall or working out fuel before a trip are mostly quick sums that mean unlocking the phone, finding an app and then forgetting the number by the next day.
en.answer: A good calculator widget lets you tap a calculation in the Home Screen widget without opening the app, keeps the keys readable in every theme, and saves the result in history you can name and search, rather than being a shortcut that opens the app or shows only the last number.
paras: Many calculator widgets are just shortcut buttons that open the app anyway; others only show the latest result. Before choosing, check whether you can really type numbers in the widget and whether what you calculate there ends up in history.
The second thing is readability. A pretty theme whose keys blend into the background makes mistakes easy on a small widget. Try the widget on the wallpaper you actually use before you decide.

CalDaily has a Home Screen widget that calculates without opening the app and follows the theme you chose in the app. Each result is saved with a name and a type, grouped by day, filtered by tool and exportable to CSV. Eight tools include tip and bill split, discount and tax, and trip fuel cost. en.h1: Copilot usage: know what is left before a big task
en.lead: Many people only find out they have used up most of their GitHub Copilot premium requests in the middle of a long task. Opening a browser, signing in and hunting for the settings page just to read one number breaks your flow.
en.answer: GitHub Copilot usage is best tracked in three parts: premium requests, chat and code completions. The most important is how many premium requests are left and exactly when they reset, because a request counts differently depending on the model you pick.
paras: Premium requests run out fastest, especially with stronger models or long-running tasks. If you have both a company account and a personal one, each has its own allowance and reset time, so it is easy to lose track of which one has room left.

A simple habit is to check usage before a big task and set a warning threshold such as 90%. When you get close, you can switch to a lighter model, move to another account, or push the heavy part until after the reset.

UsageNow shows GitHub Copilot premium requests, chat and code completions, with a countdown to the reset and the exact time in your region's format. Claude, ChatGPT Codex and Gemini sit in the same place. You can view one account's current usage free in the app; UsageNow Pro unlocks more accounts, usage alerts, widgets and Apple Watch with one purchase, no subscription.

en.title: PDF summary: facts and sources first, then the question to the AI
en.meta: Want an AI summary of a PDF but not sure it will not make things up? How to prepare a PDF before you ask: a goal, facts with sources, personal data handled. AI Brief builds this on iPhone. Free to start, one-time purchase, no subscription.
en.h1: PDF summary: prepare the facts before you ask the AI
en.lead: You drop a long PDF, such as a contract, course notes or a report, into an AI chat and ask for a summary. The answer sounds confident, but you cannot tell which page each point came from or whether the key part was lost.
en.answer: A reliable PDF summary starts before the question to the AI: state the goal, pull out the key facts with where each one came from, remove or replace personal data, and only then send it all as one tidy brief. That way the AI's answer can be checked against the source instead of taken on trust.
paras: When the whole PDF goes into the chat, the AI decides on its own what matters. With a long document, or one with tables and scans, part of the meaning gets lost, and the summary is hard to check because it does not point back to pages or passages.

It is better to decide first why you need the summary: preparing for a meeting, comparing contract terms or revising for an exam. The goal decides which facts you need. It is also worth checking the document for phone numbers, addresses and contract numbers that should not go to a third-party service.

AI Brief gathers PDFs, screenshots, files, notes and links into one brief for AI, with the goal, facts and sources each in their place. Text recognition, PDF reading, fact extraction and personal-data detection run on the iPhone, and you decide what to keep, replace or remove. Every fact keeps its source and confidence level. Copy the finished brief with one tap and paste it into any AI chat. Without a purchase, a brief can hold up to 5 sources and you can copy, send and save one brief; a one-time in-app purchase lifts those limits, with no subscription.

Free for up to 5 sources per brief; a one-time in-app purchase raises that to 50 sources and adds full version history. No subscription, no third-party ads and no tracking.

AI Brief prepares the brief for the AI: the goal, the extracted facts and their sources. You get the summary itself in whichever AI chat you paste that brief into.
Is my PDF sent to a server?
Text recognition, PDF reading and personal-data detection run on the iPhone. Only the brief you copy yourself goes to an AI service.

No. Without a purchase a brief can hold up to 5 sources; a one-time in-app purchase raises the limits. There is no subscription.

loc.title: Everyday phrases for a summer in Spain, France or Italy: learn the reply, not just the line
loc.meta: Heading to Spain, France or Italy for a holiday, a J1 alternative or an Erasmus term? Learn everyday phrases by situation, together with the reply you will hear, and review one sentence a day. DailyMate: 8,400 sentences, 47 languages, pay once.
loc.h1: Everyday phrases for Spain, France or Italy: practise the whole exchange
loc.lead: A lot of people in Ireland search for everyday phrases a few weeks before a sun holiday, an Erasmus term or a summer job on the Continent, and then freeze the first time someone answers back.
loc.answer: Choose the two or three situations you will actually face first, such as ordering at a café, checking into accommodation and asking for directions. Learn each sentence together with the reply you are most likely to hear, listen until you can say it without reading, and review one sentence a day until you travel.
paras: School Irish and a few years of Leaving Cert French or Spanish often leave people with plenty of words and very few sentences they can use at speed. The gap shows up in the second line of a conversation: you ask for a table, and the waiter asks whether you have a booking or want to sit outside. Practising the question and the likely answer together closes that gap faster than another vocabulary list.

Keep the set small and tied to places. For a holiday that is the airport, the accommodation, cafés and restaurants, shops and getting around. For an Erasmus term or a summer job, add the office or campus, the pharmacy and the doctor. Start at beginner level, and only move up once the basic pairs come out without thinking.

DailyMate works this way: 8,400 practical sentences in 47 learning languages, grouped into 14 everyday topics and 84 concrete situations, with beginner, intermediate and advanced sentences in every topic. Each sentence comes with a natural reply, can be heard with the system voice and saved as a favourite, and the Home Screen widget and Apple Watch app let you review a sentence on the bus without opening the app. It is a one-time purchase with no subscription.

faq: I did French or Spanish at school. Where should I start?
Start at beginner level in the situations you will meet first. Sentences come with replies, so you practise understanding the answer as well as saying the line.
Can I use it for languages other than European ones?
Yes. DailyMate has 47 learning languages, so the same situations are available in Japanese, Korean and many others.
Is it a subscription?
No. DailyMate is a one-time purchase.

loc.answer: 學韓文會話，先挑這一個月最可能遇到的情境（點餐、購物、搭地鐵、住宿），每次學一句完整的韓文和對方常見的回應，聽系統語音跟著說到不用看字，再往下一個情境或更高的程度走。

另一個常見卡點是聽不懂對方的回話。在餐廳說完要點的菜，店員可能接著問要不要辣、要內用還是外帶；只背自己要說的那句，對話一樣會停。所以每一句都要連同對方可能的回應一起練。

loc.h1: 開口練習：從回應對方的一句開始
loc.lead: 很多人搜尋「開口練習」，是因為讀得懂、聽得懂一點，卻一直不敢開口，或一開口就停在第二句。
loc.answer: 開口練習最容易起步的方法，是先練「回應」：聽對方的一句，例如「要內用還是外帶？」，用一句完整的話回答。一次只練一組問答，跟著系統語音說出聲，說順了再換下一組。

loc.title: To do list widget: keep a short Today list on your Home Screen through the holidays
loc.meta: Looking for a to do list widget for iPhone? From Thanksgiving to New Year, a widget only helps if the list on it is short and current. How to set it up so you actually glance at it, plus Apple Watch.
loc.h1: To do list widget: what to put on your Home Screen so you actually use it
loc.lead: You add a to-do widget, it looks great for two days, and then it either shows twenty stale tasks or something you finished last week. By mid-December you stop looking at it.
loc.answer: A to do list widget works when the list behind it is short and only holds today. Keep one Today list for the widget and a separate list for later, give each task an emoji so you can read it at a glance, tick tasks off as you finish them, and check the same list on Apple Watch when your phone is in your pocket.
paras: In the US, the stretch from Thanksgiving to New Year piles school, work deadlines, errands, gift shopping and groceries into the same few weeks. People searching for a to do list widget usually want one thing: to see the next task without opening an app. A widget can only do that if the list it shows is small enough to read in a second.

The common mistake is pointing the widget at one long master list. The top of the widget fills with old tasks, the important one is below the fold, and the widget turns into wallpaper. Splitting the season into a Today list and a Later list keeps the widget honest: only what matters today is on the Home Screen.

Mochi is a cute, cozy to-do list where every task can get its own little emoji; tap the circle when you're done. It keeps your list on a Home Screen widget and on Apple Watch, with reminders that help you stay on track and 101 themes (5 free) so the widget matches your Home Screen. The free version includes 2 lists with up to 4 tasks each, which is exactly a Today list and a Later list.
look: Does the widget show the list you choose, not every task you have ever added?
Can you read each task at a glance, for example with an emoji?
Is the same list on Apple Watch when your phone is away?
Do reminders cover the tasks with a time, such as a pickup or a deadline?
Does the widget fit the look of your Home Screen?
steps: Make two lists: Today and Later.
Keep Today to four tasks or fewer, each written as one action.
Give each task an emoji for its type: school, work, errands, groceries.
Add the widget to your Home Screen and pick a theme that matches it.
Each evening, tick off what is done and move the next tasks from Later into Today.

You see it every time you unlock your phone
Check the list without taking out your phone
Pickups and deadlines do not slip
loc.fits: Mochi fits people who want a to do list widget that is pleasant to look at and short enough to act on: emoji tasks, a satisfying tap to finish, a Home Screen widget and Apple Watch, reminders and 101 themes. It covers school, work, errands, groceries, habits and daily routines in one place.

Few enough to read in a second. A Today list of about four tasks works better than a long master list.

Yes. Mochi keeps your list on a Home Screen widget and on Apple Watch.

Yes. The free version includes 2 lists with up to 4 tasks each, 5 themes and 1 emoji set.

loc.meta: かわいいチェックリストアプリを探しているなら、見た目と同じくらい「毎日開きたくなるか」が大事。リストを短く分ける、絵文字で見分ける、ウィジェットとApple Watchで見える場所に置く。続くかわいさの選び方。
loc.h1: チェックリスト かわいい：毎日開きたくなるかわいさの選び方
loc.lead: かわいいチェックリストアプリを入れて、最初の数日は楽しい。でも項目が増えるとリストが長くなり、ホーム画面の奥にしまったまま開かなくなる――そんな経験はありませんか。
loc.answer: 続くかわいいチェックリストは、見た目に加えて「短いリスト」「ひと目で分かる目印」「見える場所」がそろっています。今日やることだけを短いリストにまとめ、項目ごとに絵文字を付け、ホーム画面のウィジェットやApple Watchでいつでも確認できるようにすると、かわいさが毎日開く理由になります。
paras: 「チェックリスト かわいい」で探す人の多くは、勉強や仕事、買い物、家事のやることを、気分よく片付けたいと思っています。見た目がかわいいことは開くきっかけになりますが、リストが長くて今日やることが埋もれると、どんなにかわいくても開かなくなります。
コツは、今日やることと後でやることを分けることです。今日のリストは数項目にしぼり、終わったら丸をタップして消していく。項目ごとに絵文字を付けておくと、勉強・買い物・家事がひと目で見分けられます。
Mochiは、タスクごとに小さな絵文字を添えられる、かわいくてやさしいToDoリストです。終わったら小さな丸をタップ。101種類のテーマ（5種類は無料）で着せ替えができ、ホーム画面のウィジェットやApple Watchで、やることをいつでも確認できます。忘れ物を防ぐリマインダーもあります。無料版では、リスト2つ（各リスト4項目まで）、テーマ5種類、絵文字1セットを使えます。

en.meta: If you want a cute checklist app, whether you will open it every day matters as much as how it looks. Split lists short, tell tasks apart with emoji, keep them visible on a widget and Apple Watch.
en.h1: Cute checklist: how to choose a cute app you will keep opening
en.lead: You install a cute checklist app and the first few days are fun. Then the list grows, today's tasks get buried, and the app stays closed on a back page of your Home Screen.
en.answer: A cute checklist that lasts has three things besides looks: a short list, a marker you can read at a glance, and a place where you can see it. Keep only today's tasks on a short list, give each task an emoji, and check it on a Home Screen widget or Apple Watch, so the cute look becomes a reason to open it every day.
paras: Most people searching for a cute checklist want to get through study, work, shopping and chores in a good mood. Looks are what make you open the app, but if the list is long and today's tasks are buried, even the cutest app stops getting opened.

The trick is to split what you do today from what can wait. Keep today's list to a few tasks and tap the circle as you finish each one. An emoji on each task lets you tell study, shopping and chores apart at a glance.

Mochi is a cute, cozy to-do list where every task can get its own little emoji; tap the circle when you're done. Switch between 101 themes (5 free) and keep your list on a Home Screen widget and Apple Watch, with reminders that help you stay on track. loc.title: Daily phrases that stick: one sentence a day from your Home Screen or watch
loc.meta: A phrase-a-day habit works when the phrase is tied to a real situation, comes with the reply you will hear and shows up where you already look. How to build it with a widget and Apple Watch. DailyMate: 8,400 sentences, 47 languages, pay once.
loc.h1: Daily phrases: build a one-sentence-a-day habit that lasts
loc.lead: Most people who search for daily phrases want a habit small enough to survive a busy week, and most phrase-a-day attempts stop after a fortnight because the app has to be opened on purpose.
loc.answer: Put one useful sentence where you already look several times a day, such as your Home Screen or your watch. Learn it with the reply you are likely to hear, listen to it once, say it aloud, and move to the next sentence only when it comes out without reading.
paras: A daily phrase only helps if it is one you will actually use. Random 'phrase of the day' feeds mix idioms, proverbs and greetings, so after a month you know thirty lines and can use three. Tying each day's sentence to one situation you will meet, such as a café, a train station or a meeting, makes the habit pay off sooner.

The habit also needs to survive days when you do not open any learning app. A widget on the Home Screen or a glance at your watch turns review into something that happens anyway, while you are checking the time or unlocking your phone. Saying the sentence aloud once, with the likely reply, is enough for that day.

DailyMate is built for this: 8,400 practical sentences in 47 learning languages, in 14 everyday topics and 84 situations, with beginner, intermediate and advanced levels. Each sentence has a natural reply and system-voice audio. The interactive Home Screen widget shows a sentence and lets you move to the next one or save it without opening the app, and the Apple Watch app shows sentences and plays the audio. It is a one-time purchase.

loc.title: Language phrases for more than one language: keep each one separate and situation-based
loc.meta: Learning phrases in two or three languages at once, for family, a partner or travel? Keep separate progress per language, learn the same situations in each, and practise each sentence with its reply. DailyMate: 47 languages, 8,400 sentences, pay once.
loc.h1: Language phrases when you are learning more than one language
loc.lead: In the UK many people need phrases in more than one language: a partner's or grandparents' language, the language of a regular holiday spot, and something for work. Phrase apps built around one language make that awkward.
loc.answer: Pick the same few everyday situations to work on in each language rather than different random lists, keep progress for each language separate so one does not crowd out the other, and practise each sentence with its likely reply. Start each new language at beginner level even if another one is already advanced.
paras: Working on the same kind of situation, say greeting family, ordering food or asking for help, in two languages lets you compare how each one says the same thing, and you are never left knowing how to do something in one language but not the other.

Keeping progress separate matters more than it seems. If your Spanish is intermediate and your Polish is a beginner's, mixing them into one list means you either bore yourself or overwhelm yourself. A separate level and set of favourites for each language keeps both moving.

DailyMate offers 47 learning languages with 8,400 practical sentences, organised into 14 everyday topics and 84 situations, each with beginner, intermediate and advanced sentences and a natural reply. Progress and favourites are kept separately for each learning language, sentences can be heard with the system voice, and a Home Screen widget and Apple Watch app make quick review easy. It is a one-time purchase, not a subscription per language.

It is a one-time purchase, not a subscription per language.

loc.h1: ひとこと練習：近場の海外旅行は現地語の「返し」を一言だけ
loc.lead: 韓国、台湾、タイなど近場の海外旅行では、英語が通じても、現地の言葉で「ありがとう」「これをください」と一言返すだけで店員の表情が変わります。でも何を練習すればいいか分からず、結局英語だけで済ませてしまう人がほとんどです。
loc.answer: 現地語は全部を学ぼうとせず、店員によく言われる一言と、それに返す一言のペアだけを練習します。出発前の数日、韓国語・中国語・タイ語などで1日数組ずつ声に出し、音声の速度を落として聞き取りから慣らしておくのが効率的です。
paras: 近場の旅行で現地語を使う場面は限られています。お店で「いらっしゃいませ」と言われたとき、会計で袋が要るか聞かれたとき、屋台で注文するとき。この数場面の一往復だけで、旅の印象はかなり変わります。
韓国語、中国語、タイ語は、日本語話者には発音や声調が難しく感じられます。だからこそ文字を読むより、音声を遅めの速度で何度か聞き、相手の一言を聞き取れるようにしてから自分の返しを言う順番が効きます。

en.title: One-line practice for trips to Korea, Taiwan or Thailand: learn the local reply
en.meta: Even if your English works, answering in the local language in Seoul, Taipei or Bangkok changes the trip. Practise what staff say and a short reply as pairs, a few a day, in the local language. DailyMate Lite: the Traveler topic at Beginner level is free in every language.
en.h1: One-line practice: just the local reply for nearby trips
en.lead: On short trips from Japan to Korea, Taiwan or Thailand, English often works, but replying with a local thank you or this one, please changes how staff respond. Most travellers do not know what to practise and fall back on English.
en.answer: Do not try to learn the whole language. Practise only what staff commonly say and one reply, in Korean, Chinese, Thai or wherever you are going, a few pairs a day in the days before you leave, with slowed audio first.
paras: Local-language moments on short trips are few: a greeting at the door, being asked about a bag at the till, ordering at a stall. Those few exchanges change the feel of the trip.
Korean, Chinese and Thai can feel hard to pronounce for Japanese speakers, so listening at a slower speed until you can catch the other person's line, then replying, works better than reading.

DailyMate Lite is built for this: 8,400 cue-and-reply pairs in 50 learning languages, 14 topics and 84 situations at three levels, with adjustable-speed system voices, a widget and Apple Watch. The Traveler topic at Beginner level is free in every language; the rest unlocks with a one-time purchase. No account, third-party ads or tracking.
